question: Under Maryland law, when does a brokerage relationship between a licensee and a client legally commence?
choice_a: At the time the client enters into a brokerage agreement with the licensee
choice_b: At the time the client first speaks with the licensee by phone
choice_c: At the time the licensee shows the client a property
choice_d: At the time the client signs a contract of sale
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(a) provides that a brokerage relationship commences at the time a client enters into a brokerage agreement with a licensee, and continues until completion of performance, expiration, mutual termination, or default.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(a)

question: A Maryland listing agreement (seller/lessor brokerage agreement) must include which of the following terms?
choice_a: A clause allowing the agreement to renew automatically each year unless canceled
choice_b: A definite date on which the agreement automatically terminates
choice_c: A requirement that the seller use only the listing broker's in-house lender
choice_d: A waiver of the seller's right to cancel the agreement
explanation: §17-534(b) requires a seller/lessor brokerage agreement to contain a definite date on which the agreement automatically terminates, among other required terms. Open-ended or automatically renewing listing agreements are not permitted.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(b)

question: Besides a definite termination date, what else must a Maryland seller/lessor brokerage (listing) agreement specify?
choice_a: The specific buyer who will ultimately purchase the property
choice_b: The appraised value of the property as determined by a licensed appraiser
choice_c: The amount of compensation, terms for cooperating with and compensating other brokers, the events that entitle the broker to a commission, and cancellation provisions
choice_d: A list of all other brokers licensed in the seller's county
explanation: Under §17-534(b), a seller/lessor brokerage agreement must state the compensation to be paid, the terms of cooperation and compensation-sharing with other brokers, the events that trigger entitlement to a commission, and provisions for cancellation.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(b)

question: A Maryland buyer/lessee brokerage agreement must disclose which of the following regarding compensation?
choice_a: Only that the buyer's agent will be paid solely by the seller
choice_b: That compensation may never be shared with the listing broker
choice_c: That the buyer must pay a fixed statutory commission set by the Real Estate Commission
choice_d: The amount of compensation, whether expressed as a percentage, a flat dollar amount, or a combination, and whether the licensee is authorized to receive compensation from a third party along with the client's rights concerning that compensation
explanation: §17-534(c) requires a buyer/lessee brokerage agreement to state the compensation amount (as a percentage, dollar amount, or combination), whether the licensee is authorized to receive compensation from a third party, and the client's rights regarding such third-party compensation, along with a termination date, commission-triggering events, and cancellation provisions.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(c)

question: Under Maryland law, does the mere payment of compensation to a real estate licensee, by itself, establish that a brokerage relationship exists?
choice_a: No, payment of compensation is not determinative of and does not by itself create a brokerage relationship
choice_b: Yes, any payment automatically creates a full brokerage relationship
choice_c: Yes, but only if the payment exceeds $500
choice_d: No, because brokerage relationships in Maryland must always be oral
explanation: §17-534(e) specifically states that payment of compensation is not determinative of whether a brokerage relationship exists between a person and a licensee, and does not by itself establish such a relationship.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(e)

question: After a Maryland brokerage relationship terminates, what duties does the licensee still owe to the former client?
choice_a: No duties whatsoever survive termination
choice_b: To account for trust money and to maintain confidentiality of client information, unless the client consents to disclosure or the information becomes publicly available
choice_c: A continuing duty to find the client a new licensee
choice_d: A duty to represent the client again for free in the next transaction
explanation: §17-534(d) provides that after a brokerage relationship ends, the licensee has no further duties to the former client except to account for trust money in a timely manner and to maintain the confidentiality of client information, unless the client consents to disclosure or the information becomes public.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-534(d)

question: May a Maryland brokerage agreement impose duties on a licensee beyond the baseline statutory duties listed in §17-532?
choice_a: No, brokerage agreements may never add to the statutory duties
choice_b: Yes, but only if approved in advance by the Real Estate Commission on a case-by-case basis
choice_c: Yes, §17-531 makes clear the statute does not prohibit a licensee and client from agreeing to additional duties beyond those specified in §17-532
choice_d: No, additional duties can only be created by a separate power of attorney
explanation: §17-531 states that the subtitle does not prohibit a licensee and a client from entering into a brokerage agreement that imposes duties and obligations on the licensee in addition to those specified in §17-532.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-531

question: By what deadline must a Maryland real estate licensee provide the written disclosure of whom the licensee represents in a residential transaction?
choice_a: At closing, at the same time the deed is signed
choice_b: Within 30 days after the licensee is first contacted
choice_c: Only if the other party specifically requests it in writing
choice_d: Not later than the first scheduled face-to-face contact with the buyer/lessee or seller/lessor
explanation: §17-530(b) requires that the written disclosure of brokerage relationship occur not later than the first scheduled face-to-face contact with the buyer/lessee or seller/lessor, with an alternate method specified when the first contact is not face-to-face.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(b)

question: Under §17-530, is a licensee excused from making the written brokerage relationship disclosure to a party with whom the licensee already has a written brokerage agreement?
choice_a: Yes, the disclosure requirement does not apply where the parties already have an existing written brokerage agreement
choice_b: No, the disclosure must always be repeated even with an existing written agreement
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial transactions, never residential
choice_d: No, unless the existing agreement is more than one year old
explanation: §17-530(a) provides an exception to the mandatory written disclosure of brokerage relationship where the licensee and the party already have a written brokerage agreement, since the representation is already established and documented.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(a)

question: If a Maryland licensee's first contact with a customer is not face-to-face (for example, by phone or email), how must the brokerage relationship disclosure be handled?
choice_a: No disclosure is required until an in-person meeting eventually occurs
choice_b: The licensee must disclose through the same medium used for that first contact
choice_c: The licensee may wait until the contract of sale is signed
choice_d: The disclosure obligation is waived entirely for non-face-to-face contact
explanation: §17-530(a)-(b) requires that when the first contact is not face-to-face, the licensee must make the disclosure through the medium of that first contact (e.g., in writing by mail, email, or comparable means), rather than waiting for an in-person meeting.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(a)-(b)

question: When a Maryland seller's agent is showing a property at an open house to members of the public with no individual buyer's agent present, how may the disclosure of brokerage relationship be satisfied?
choice_a: It cannot be satisfied at an open house; each visitor must sign a separate written agreement first
choice_b: The seller must personally greet and disclose to each visitor
choice_c: By conspicuous notice, such as posting the disclosure where visitors to the open house can readily see it
choice_d: No disclosure is required at open houses under any circumstances
explanation: §17-530(b) allows a licensee holding property open to the public to satisfy the disclosure obligation through conspicuous notice, rather than an individualized face-to-face disclosure to every visitor.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(b)

question: In a Maryland transaction where a subagent is involved, what must the subagent disclose to the buyer or lessee?
choice_a: That the subagent represents the buyer exclusively
choice_b: Nothing, because subagents have no disclosure duty
choice_c: Only that the subagent is licensed, without stating who is represented
choice_d: In writing, that the subagent represents the seller or lessor
explanation: §17-530(c) requires a subagent to disclose in writing to the buyer or lessee that the subagent represents the interests of the seller or lessor, not the buyer.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(c)

question: If a Maryland transaction has neither a subagent nor a buyer's agent, who is responsible for making the written brokerage relationship disclosure to the buyer/lessee?
choice_a: The seller's agent must provide the written disclosure directly to the buyer/lessee
choice_b: No disclosure is required if there is no subagent or buyer's agent
choice_c: The Maryland Real Estate Commission makes the disclosure on the parties' behalf
choice_d: The title company handling closing must provide the disclosure
explanation: §17-530(d) requires that when there is no subagent or buyer's agent involved, the seller's agent must give the required written disclosure directly to the buyer or lessee.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(d)

question: If a Maryland transaction has no seller's agent, who must provide the written brokerage relationship disclosure to the seller or lessor?
choice_a: The buyer must personally disclose to the seller
choice_b: The buyer's agent must disclose in writing to the seller/lessor
choice_c: No one is required to disclose to the seller in that scenario
choice_d: Only the settlement/title agent is required to disclose
explanation: §17-530(e) requires that when there is no seller's agent, the buyer's agent must provide the required written disclosure to the seller or lessor.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(e)

question: Under §17-530(f), the written brokerage relationship disclosure given to Maryland consumers must explain which of the following?
choice_a: Only the current interest rate environment for mortgage financing
choice_b: The specific commission split between the listing and selling brokers
choice_c: The differences between the types of agents (such as seller's agent, buyer's agent, subagent, dual agent, and intra-company agent) and the duties each owes, including how to file a complaint with the Commission
choice_d: The seller's original purchase price for the property
explanation: §17-530(f) requires the disclosure to explain, among other things, the differences between the various categories of real estate agents and the duties owed under each, along with information on how a consumer may file a complaint with the Real Estate Commission.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530(f)

question: Under Maryland's dual agency statute, may a licensee act as a dual agent representing both the seller and the buyer in the same transaction?
choice_a: Never under any circumstances in Maryland
choice_b: Yes, automatically, as long as the licensee tells both parties verbally at closing
choice_c: Only if the transaction involves commercial property
choice_d: Only with the informed, written consent of all parties to the transaction
explanation: §17-530.1 prohibits a licensee from acting as a dual agent except with the informed, written consent of all parties to the transaction, given after required disclosures about the nature of dual agency.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530.1

question: When acting as a properly consented dual agent in Maryland, what must a licensee disclose to both the buyer and seller about the nature of that representation?
choice_a: That the dual agent does not owe undivided loyalty to either the seller or the buyer, and that a conflict of interest may exist because their interests could be different or adverse
choice_b: That the dual agent automatically prioritizes whichever party pays the higher commission
choice_c: That dual agency guarantees a lower purchase price for the buyer
choice_d: That once dual agency is established, either party loses the right to withdraw consent
explanation: §17-530.1 requires that dual agency disclosures explain that the dual agent does not owe undivided loyalty to either party and that a conflict of interest may exist because the buyer's and seller's interests can differ or be adverse.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530.1

question: In a Maryland dual agency arrangement using designated intra-company agents, what confidentiality restriction applies?
choice_a: Intra-company agents must share all information freely between both sides to ensure fairness
choice_b: An intra-company agent representing one party may not disclose that party's confidential information to the other side of the transaction, except as otherwise required by law
choice_c: Confidentiality rules do not apply once intra-company agents are designated
choice_d: Only the broker, not the intra-company agents, is bound by confidentiality
explanation: §17-530.1 provides that an intra-company agent designated to represent one party in a dual agency situation may not disclose that party's confidential information to the buyer or seller on the other side, except as required by law.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530.1

question: What formatting requirements does §17-530.2 impose on the Maryland Real Estate Commission's standard agency disclosure and dual agency consent forms?
choice_a: The forms may be handwritten in any font size the licensee prefers
choice_b: The forms must be printed exclusively in legal-size format
choice_c: The forms must be written in clear, everyday language, appropriately divided and captioned by section, and printed in at least 10-point type
choice_d: There are no formatting requirements imposed by statute
explanation: §17-530.2(b) requires that the Commission's standard disclosure and consent forms be written clearly using common, everyday language, be appropriately divided and captioned by section, and be printed in at least 10-point type.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530.2(b)

question: Who is responsible for preparing and providing the standard agency disclosure and dual agency consent forms that Maryland licensees use?
choice_a: Each individual brokerage must design its own unique form with no Commission oversight
choice_b: The buyer's attorney is responsible for drafting the disclosure form
choice_c: The county clerk of court issues the required forms
choice_d: The Maryland Real Estate Commission prepares and provides these standard forms to all licensees
explanation: §17-530.2(b)(1) requires the Real Estate Commission to prepare and provide the standard disclosure form and the standard dual agency consent form to all licensees in the state, and COMAR 09.11.08.01 requires those Commission-provided model forms to be used in applicable transactions.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-530.2(b)(1); COMAR 09.11.08.01

question: Under COMAR's Code of Ethics provisions on relations to the client, may a Maryland licensee accept compensation from more than one party to the same transaction?
choice_a: Only with the full knowledge and consent of all parties involved in the transaction
choice_b: Yes, at any time, without informing anyone
choice_c: No, it is absolutely prohibited under all circumstances, even with consent
choice_d: Only if the amounts received from each party are identical
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.C provides that a licensee may not accept compensation from more than one party to a transaction without the full knowledge and consent of all parties, since undisclosed dual compensation creates an undisclosed conflict of interest.

question: Under Maryland's Code of Ethics, if a licensee wants to purchase a property for their own account, what must the licensee do before submitting an offer to the seller?
choice_a: Nothing; a licensee buying for personal use has no special disclosure obligation
choice_b: Disclose in writing to the seller/lessor that the purchaser is a licensed real estate licensee, before the offer is submitted
choice_c: Wait until after closing to reveal their license status
choice_d: Obtain a waiver from the Real Estate Commission before making any offer
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.D requires a licensee acquiring an interest in real property for their own account to disclose their license status in writing to the seller or lessor before the offer is submitted, so the seller is aware they are dealing with a licensed professional.

question: Does the Maryland conflict-of-interest disclosure requirement for a licensee acquiring property for their own account also extend to purchases made by the licensee's immediate family or an entity in which the licensee holds an ownership interest?
choice_a: No, the disclosure obligation applies strictly and only to the individual licensee personally
choice_b: No, family purchases are entirely exempt from Maryland real estate regulation
choice_c: Yes, the same written disclosure obligation applies to acquisitions by the licensee's family members, affiliated employees or team members, and entities in which the licensee has an ownership interest
choice_d: Yes, but only if the family member is also a licensed salesperson
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.D extends the written disclosure requirement to acquisitions by the licensee's defined family members, affiliated employees or team members, and to entities in which the licensee has an ownership interest, to prevent circumventing the conflict-of-interest disclosure.

question: When a Maryland licensee is selling or leasing property that the licensee (or a covered family member/affiliated entity) owns, how must the ownership interest be disclosed to prospective buyers or tenants?
choice_a: Verbally only, at the final walk-through
choice_b: Disclosure is not required if the property is listed by a different agent at the same brokerage
choice_c: Only if a prospective buyer specifically asks whether the seller is a licensee
choice_d: In writing, such as through the multiple listing service or other equally effective written notice
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.D requires that when a licensee is offering their own property (or that of a covered family member or affiliated entity) for sale or lease, the ownership interest be disclosed in writing, such as through the MLS listing or other equally effective written notice.

question: For purposes of Maryland's conflict-of-interest disclosure rule on a licensee's interest in property, which of the following relationships is included within the regulation's definition of 'family'?
choice_a: Spouse or domestic partner, children and stepchildren (and their spouses), parents, siblings, grandparents, and grandchildren
choice_b: Only the licensee's spouse; no other relatives are covered
choice_c: Any person who has ever worked at the same brokerage, regardless of relation
choice_d: Cousins and in-laws only
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.D defines 'family' for purposes of the conflict-of-interest disclosure rule to include a spouse or domestic partner, children and stepchildren (including their spouses), parents, siblings, grandparents, and grandchildren.

question: When a Maryland licensee prepares a competitive market analysis (CMA) for a client, and the licensee has a personal interest in one of the comparable properties used, what must the licensee do?
choice_a: Nothing, because a CMA is never shown to the client
choice_b: Conspicuously disclose that the CMA is not an appraisal and separately disclose the licensee's personal property interest in any comparable used
choice_c: Relabel the CMA as an official appraisal to avoid confusion
choice_d: Refuse to prepare the CMA if any comparable involves a personal interest
explanation: COMAR 09.11.02.02.F requires that a CMA conspicuously disclose it is not an appraisal and is intended only to assist in listing or pricing decisions, and separately requires disclosure of any personal property interest the licensee holds in a comparable property used in the analysis.
